questions.question_text: The price of tea rises by 20% and the quantity of coffee demanded rises by 8%. The cross elasticity of demand and the relationship between the goods are:
questions.explanation: Ec = 8/20 = +0.4; a positive sign means the goods are substitutes.

questions.question_text: When the price of a car rises sharply, demand for petrol falls. This happens because:
options: Petrol is an inferior good in consumption
Cars and petrol are used together as complements
Cars and petrol are close substitutes in use
Petrol is a Giffen good in the market
questions.explanation: A rise in the price of a complement reduces demand for the other good.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the right?
options: A fall in the price of a substitute good
A fall in the price of the good itself
A rise in the price of a complementary good
questions.explanation: Higher income raises demand at every price.

questions.question_text: Income rises by 10% and quantity demanded of a good rises by 4%. The good is:
options: A necessity with income elasticity of 0.4
A Giffen good with unitary elasticity
A luxury with income elasticity of 2.5
An inferior good with negative elasticity
questions.explanation: Ey = 4/10 = 0.4, between 0 and 1.

questions.question_text: The market demand schedule is obtained by:
options: Selecting the highest bid for each unit of the good
Adding the prices that individual buyers are willing to pay
Adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price
Averaging the prices that individual buyers are willing to pay
questions.explanation: Horizontal summation of individual demands.

questions.question_text: At a price of Rs 10, buyers A, B and C demand 4, 6 and 10 units. The market demand at Rs 10 is:
Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the demand for a commodity?
options: Cost of production of the seller
questions.explanation: Cost of production affects supply.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the law of demand is correct?
options: It holds only when consumer incomes also fall at the same time
It states that quantity demanded falls as price rises, other things equal
It states that quantity demanded rises as price rises, other things equal
It applies equally to Giffen goods and to normal goods
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related ceteris paribus.

questions.question_text: An exception to the law of demand is:
options: A substitute good such as coffee
A Veblen good such as a luxury watch
A perishable good such as vegetables
questions.explanation: Higher price increases the prestige value and thus demand.

questions.question_text: Giffen goods differ from Veblen goods in that Giffen goods are:
options: Goods with a perfectly inelastic demand curve
Inferior goods that take a large share of income
Goods whose demand rises due to expected inflation
Luxury goods bought for show and status
questions.explanation: Veblen goods are prestige goods; Giffen goods are poor man's staples.

questions.question_text: The price of a good falls from Rs 20 to Rs 18 and quantity demanded rises from 100 to 130. Price elasticity (percentage method) is:
Price rises from Rs 40 to Rs 50 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 150. Ed is:
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = 25%, %ΔP = 25%, so Ed = 1 (unitary).

questions.question_text: The arc elasticity between (P = 10, Q = 40) and (P = 8, Q = 50) using mid-points is:
Ed = 2 and price falls by 5%. Quantity demanded will:
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = Ed × %ΔP.

questions.question_text: If a price fall leaves total expenditure unchanged, demand is:
questions.explanation: TE is constant only when Ed = 1.

questions.question_text: If price falls and total expenditure falls, demand is:
questions.explanation: Ed < 1 reduces expenditure when price falls.

questions.question_text: The point on a linear demand curve where Ed = 1 is the:
options: Point of tangency with an IC
questions.explanation: Lower segment equals upper segment at the midpoint.

questions.question_text: On a straight-line demand curve, the elasticity at a point two-thirds of the way down from the Y-axis (lower segment : upper segment = 1 : 2) is:
questions.explanation: Ed = lower/upper = 1/2.

questions.question_text: Which of the following goods is likely to have the lowest price elasticity of demand?
options: Branded packaged biscuits with many rivals
questions.explanation: Necessity, small expenditure share and few substitutes.

questions.question_text: Demand tends to be more elastic when:
options: The good takes a very small share of income
The good is a necessity with no substitute
The good is habitual or addictive
The time period considered is longer
questions.explanation: Consumers have time to find substitutes.

questions.question_text: A 10% rise in the price of a good reduces quantity demanded by 25%. The demand is:
A good has Ed = 0.5. Total revenue will rise when the seller:
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, price and revenue move together.

questions.question_text: If a good has elastic demand, MR is:
questions.explanation: MR = P(1 − 1/Ed) > 0 when Ed > 1.

questions.question_text: Given price Rs 20 and Ed = 4, marginal revenue is:
Given AR = Rs 30 and MR = Rs 20, elasticity of demand is:
Demand curve of a firm under perfect competition is:
questions.explanation: It sells at the market price.

questions.question_text: The demand for life-saving drugs is likely to be:
questions.explanation: Few substitutes and urgent need.

questions.question_text: A government wants more tax revenue from a good with a given rate of tax. It should tax a good with:
questions.explanation: Quantity falls little, so revenue rises.

questions.question_text: The "paradox of poverty" in agriculture arises because:
options: Farmers cut output sharply whenever the price of their crop is low
A bumper crop can lower farmers' total income, as demand for food is inelastic
Farm produce cannot be stored for sale in later seasons
Demand for food is highly elastic with respect to price
questions.explanation: Price falls proportionately more than the quantity sold rises.

questions.question_text: For the same rise in income, demand for good X rises from 100 to 130 and for good Y from 100 to 105. Income elasticity is:
options: Higher for Y, which is the more income-elastic good
Negative for Y as its demand rose by a smaller amount
Higher for X, which is the more income-elastic good
Equal for the two goods since income rose equally
questions.explanation: A larger proportionate change in quantity for the same income change means higher elasticity.

questions.question_text: A negative income elasticity is a feature of:
questions.explanation: Demand falls as income rises.

questions.question_text: If cross elasticity between two goods is zero, the goods are:
questions.explanation: Change in the price of one has no effect on the other.

questions.question_text: A fall in the price of petrol raises demand for cars. The cross elasticity is:
questions.explanation: Complements have negative cross elasticity.

questions.question_text: "Extension of demand" is caused by:
options: A fall in the price of the good
A fall in the price of a substitute
questions.explanation: It is a movement along the same curve.

questions.question_text: "Increase in demand" is shown by:
options: A rightward shift of the curve
A downward movement along the curve
A leftward shift of the curve
An upward movement along the curve
questions.explanation: More is demanded at each price.

questions.question_text: Which single change would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the left?
options: A fall in the cost of producing the good
A fall in the good's own price in the market
An increase in the number of sellers
A fall in the incomes of consumers
questions.explanation: Lower income reduces demand at each price; the others move along the curve or shift supply.

questions.question_text: A rise in the price of coffee shifts the demand curve for tea:
options: Right, as the goods are complements
Left, as the goods are substitutes
Right, as the goods are substitutes
Left, as the goods are complements
questions.explanation: Tea demand rises as consumers shift away from coffee.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a movement along the demand curve rather than a shift?
options: Contraction of demand because of a rise in the own price
Increase in demand because of a favourable fashion
Decrease in demand because of a fall in a substitute's price
Increase in demand because of higher income
questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves along the curve.

questions.question_text: Suppose demand is Qd = 100 − 2P. At P = 20 the quantity demanded is:
For Qd = 100 − 2P, the price elasticity at P = 20 is:
For Qd = 100 − 2P, demand is unitary elastic at P =:
A market demand curve is flatter than individual demand curves because:
options: Individuals buy larger quantities when the price is high
All individuals in the market have the same income level
Market demand does not depend on the price of the good
More buyers enter at lower prices, so quantity rises sharply
questions.explanation: Summing quantities at every price spreads the curve horizontally.

questions.question_text: The demand curve derived from the marginal utility curve slopes downward because of:
questions.explanation: Willingness to pay falls as consumption increases.

questions.question_text: A consumer buys more of a good when its price falls partly because she feels richer. This is the:
questions.explanation: Real income rises when price falls.

questions.question_text: Which of the following goods is a likely example of derived demand?
options: Demand for ice cream by children
Demand for a movie ticket by a student
Demand for a wristwatch as a gift
Demand for steel by an automobile manufacturer
questions.explanation: Steel is demanded because cars are demanded.

questions.question_text: Composite demand arises when:
options: The good is demanded at one price only
The good is demanded by the government
A good has several alternative uses
questions.explanation: E.g., milk or steel with many uses.

questions.question_text: When income is redistributed from the rich to the poor, demand for necessities generally:
questions.explanation: The poor spend a larger share on necessities.

questions.question_text: Expectation of a future price rise tends to:
questions.explanation: Consumers buy more now.

questions.question_text: Which of these describes "advertising elasticity" of demand?
options: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in advertising spending
Responsiveness of the price level to a change in the tax rate
Responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price
Responsiveness of national income to a change in total output
questions.explanation: It measures the promotional effect on quantity demanded.

questions.question_text: An advertisement campaign that raises sales at every price will:
options: Shift the demand curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the left
questions.explanation: It increases demand.

questions.question_text: A seller facing elastic demand who wants to raise revenue should:
questions.explanation: Quantity rises proportionately more than price falls.

questions.question_text: If a firm faces unitary elastic demand, total revenue as price changes is:
questions.explanation: Revenue is maximum where Ed = 1.

questions.question_text: The tax burden falls more on the side of the market that has:
questions.explanation: The side that cannot easily switch bears more of it.

questions.question_text: A fall in the exchange rate (devaluation) improves the trade balance if the sum of elasticities of exports and imports is:
questions.explanation: The Marshall–Lerner condition.

questions.question_text: If the price of good A rises by 10% and the quantity demanded of good B rises by 3%, B and A are:
questions.explanation: Positive cross elasticity.

questions.question_text: Demand for a good is perfectly inelastic. A price rise:
options: Reduces quantity by a large amount
questions.explanation: Ed = 0, vertical demand curve.

questions.question_text: If the demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, elasticity is:
questions.explanation: Total expenditure is constant at every price.

questions.question_text: Total expenditure method says demand is elastic if price and total expenditure move:
questions.explanation: A price fall raises expenditure when Ed > 1.

questions.question_text: A price fall from Rs 5 to Rs 4 raises sales from 50 to 60 units, so total revenue changes from Rs 250 to Rs 240. Over this range demand is:
questions.explanation: When a price cut lowers total revenue, demand is inelastic.

questions.question_text: A seller raises price from Rs 50 to Rs 60 and total revenue rises. Over that range demand is:
questions.explanation: Revenue and price move in the same direction when Ed < 1.

questions.question_text: For Qd = 40 − 4P, the arc elasticity (mid-point) when price rises from Rs 5 to Rs 6 is about:
"Perishable goods" such as vegetables tend to have:
options: Inelastic demand and supply in the short run
questions.explanation: Cannot be stored; need is regular.

questions.question_text: A good with many close substitutes has demand that is:
questions.explanation: Consumers can switch easily.

questions.question_text: Demand for a product tends to be more elastic in the long run because:
options: Prices of goods are fixed by the government over time
Consumers' incomes keep falling as time passes by
Consumers have time to find substitutes and change habits
The supply of goods stays fixed for a long period
questions.explanation: Adjustment to a price change takes time.

questions.question_text: A good which forms a very small portion of income, like a matchbox, usually has demand that is:
questions.explanation: Price changes hardly affect the budget.

questions.question_text: Veblen goods appear to violate the law of demand because:
options: Their supply cannot be increased in the short run
Buyers take a higher price as a mark of status and buy more
They are necessities with no available substitutes
They are inferior goods taking a large share of income
questions.explanation: Price itself signals prestige.

questions.question_text: The Giffen paradox was first observed in the case of:
options: A staple food consumed by poor households
Gold held as a store of value
Luxury cars bought by wealthy households
Mobile phones sold in urban markets
questions.explanation: Sir Robert Giffen noted it for staple foods of the poor.

questions.question_text: Which of the following will shift the demand curve for tea leftward?
options: A fall in the price of tea
A fall in income of consumers
A rise in the price of coffee
questions.explanation: Lower income reduces demand for a normal good.

questions.question_text: If demand rises and supply is unchanged, equilibrium price:
questions.explanation: Excess demand pushes price up.

questions.question_text: A demand curve of the form P × Q = 600 implies:
questions.explanation: Total expenditure is constant.

questions.question_text: The relation between TR, MR and elasticity: TR is maximum where:
questions.explanation: At this point Ed = 1.

questions.question_text: If a monopolist faces Ed = 0.8 at a price, he should:
questions.explanation: MR is negative when Ed < 1; reducing output raises revenue.

questions.question_text: Income elasticity of a luxury good is:
questions.explanation: Demand rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.question_text: When Y changes from 200 to 250 and quantity demanded changes from 40 to 60, income elasticity (percentage method) is:
The percentage method of elasticity is unsuitable when:
questions.explanation: It gives different values for rises and falls; the arc method is preferred.

questions.question_text: A firm lowers price by 10% and its revenue rises. This shows that demand over this range is:
questions.explanation: Revenue and price move in opposite directions.

questions.question_text: Which statement best explains why the demand for salt is inelastic?
options: It is an inferior good whose demand falls as income rises
It takes a small share of income and has no close substitute
It is a luxury with many close substitutes available
Its price changes very frequently from week to week
questions.explanation: Cheap, necessary and no substitute.

questions.question_text: A seller wants to know the effect of a Rs 2 rise in price on revenue. He needs to know:
questions.explanation: Elasticity tells the direction of the revenue change.

questions.question_text: When a good is in joint demand, a rise in the price of one good will:
options: Reduce the demand for the other
Not change the demand for the other
Raise the demand for the other
questions.explanation: Goods demanded together are complements.

questions.question_text: Which of these best describes "competitive demand"?
options: Demand by competing governments for the same resources
Demand for goods that can be used in place of each other
Demand by rival exporters in a foreign market
Demand for goods that are used together as complements
questions.explanation: E.g., tea and coffee.

questions.question_text: Which statement is true about the demand for inferior goods?
questions.explanation: Income elasticity is negative.

questions.question_text: An income elasticity of demand between 0 and 1 indicates that the good is a:
questions.explanation: Quantity rises less than proportionately with income.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a "ceteris paribus" assumption in the law of demand?
questions.explanation: Everything except the price of the good is held constant.

questions.question_text: If a consumer's demand for a good is unaffected by changes in income, the good's income elasticity is:
questions.explanation: Neutral good.

questions.question_text: The demand curve for a good with unit elasticity at all prices on the graph looks like:
questions.explanation: PQ is constant.

questions.question_text: When price increases from Rs 20 to Rs 22 and total revenue rises, demand is:
questions.explanation: Revenue rises with price when Ed < 1.

questions.question_text: Perfect competition firms face demand that is:
questions.explanation: They are price takers.

questions.question_text: "A fall in income by 5% reduces demand by 15%." Income elasticity is:
questions.explanation: 15/5 = 3, a luxury.

questions.question_text: Price elasticity of demand will be higher for a good:
questions.explanation: Substitution possibilities raise elasticity.

questions.question_text: A demand curve's slope is not the same as its elasticity because elasticity depends on:
options: Only the slope of the curve at that point
The slope and the ratio of price to quantity
Only the quantity at which the good is sold
Only the price at which the good sells
questions.explanation: Ed = (1/slope) × (P/Q).

questions.question_text: Along a downward-sloping straight-line demand curve, elasticity:
options: Is zero at all the points of the curve
Is higher at high prices and lower at low prices
Is lower at high prices and higher at low prices
Is the same at all the points of the curve
questions.explanation: Elasticity falls as one moves down the curve.

questions.question_text: A consumer's demand for X rises from 20 to 24 when his income rises from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,100. Ey is:
Which of the following would an economist expect to be elastic?
options: Demand for a particular brand of cola
questions.explanation: Many close substitutes.

questions.question_text: If cross elasticity of demand between X and Y is −2, then a 10% fall in the price of Y will:
The demand curve slopes downward partly because:
options: Taxes on the good fall when price falls
Cost of production falls when output rises
Supply of the good rises when price falls
Lower prices attract new buyers into the market
questions.explanation: New consumers enter at lower prices.

questions.question_text: Price elasticity of demand is the ratio of:
options: Percentage change in quantity demanded to percentage change in price
Percentage change in price to percentage change in quantity
Absolute change in quantity to absolute change in price
Change in income to change in quantity
questions.explanation: Ed = %ΔQ/%ΔP.

questions.question_text: When the price of a good rises, the demand for a Giffen good:
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded rises because the income effect dominates.

questions.question_text: A rise in the price of rice, a staple for the poor, increases their consumption of rice. This is consistent with:
questions.explanation: Strong negative income effect.

questions.question_text: "Ceteris paribus" is needed in demand analysis because:
options: Income of consumers never changes over time
Many factors affect demand and we isolate the effect of price
Supply of the good is fixed in every period
Price has no real effect on the quantity demanded
questions.explanation: It isolates a single cause.

questions.question_text: If a price rise from Rs 10 to Rs 11 reduces demand from 100 to 90, Ed (percentage method) is:
